taxonomyNote: NatureServe names it Eastern Cricket Frog and treats A. blanchardi as a separate species (Gamble et al. 2008); ADW's Northern Cricket Frog account gives a wider range extending to Texas, Mexico and Ontario, consistent with the older combined concept.
fieldMarks: Small frog, 22-29 mm; eastern animals are smaller (22-26 mm) than western ones (24-29 mm).
Polymorphic dorsal stripe that can be green, red or grey (green most common); stripe is absent on tadpoles and appears after metamorphosis.
Compared with the southern cricket frog it is larger and stockier, with a blunter snout, shorter legs, more toe webbing and more prominent warts.
behavior: Call is a series of short clicks given in rapid bouts; males lower call pitch to assert dominance.
Diet is mostly small terrestrial insects plus some spiders, taken opportunistically.
Diurnal in cool weather and active day and night in warm months; inactive in the coldest months in the north, brumating in bank crevices, under logs or vegetation; moves after heavy rain.
habitat: Edges of sunny marshes, marshy ponds and small slow-moving streams in open country; eggs and larvae develop in shallow water.
Hibernates underground on land near water, sometimes communally.
range: NatureServe lists it in the eastern US from New York and Pennsylvania south to Florida, Alabama, Mississippi and Louisiana; it is not recorded for Canada in that source.

lookalikes.name: Southern cricket frog
lookalikes.howToTell: Southern is smaller and more slender, with a more pointed snout, longer legs, less toe webbing, and a dark longitudinal stripe on the rear of the thigh.
